formNote: The graph began as a dancer; “not have” is a sound loan. The four dots at the bottom of the modern form are generally explained as a reshaping of the dancer’s lower body, not 灬 “fire”.
summary: Oracle-bone 無 pictures a dancer holding plumes or branches. The graph was borrowed for the sound of a word meaning “there is not”, and the dance moved to 舞. In philosophy 無 becomes the indeterminate from which determinate things arise.
placement: On the origin — the attractor’s third equilibrium, an unstable point from which trajectories depart and which they never settle back into.

satellites.title: A Dancer, Borrowed for “Not”
satellites.evidence: Shang graphs show a figure holding ornaments or branches in both hands, the ancestor of 舞, “dance”. 無 came to write “not have” by phonetic borrowing (假借): the sound, not the picture, carried the new meaning.

satellites.title: Reading Emptiness Through 無
satellites.evidence: Early Chinese Buddhists read Prajñāpāramitā thought through Daoist 無 — a method later called 格義, “matching concepts”; Lokakṣema even rendered tathatā, “suchness”, as 本無. Sengzhao’s essay rejects the “Original Non-being” school: emptiness (空, śūnyatā) means things lack independent existence, not that they do not exist — neither simply 有 nor 無.
satellites.caveat: The standard rendering of śūnyatā is 空, not 無.

satellites.title: Absence and Usable Emptiness
satellites.evidence: Malay tiada and French néant name plain absence; Malay kosong, “empty”, names the hollow of a vessel. Daodejing ch. 11 locates the usefulness of a cup or a room in exactly that unoccupied space.

satellites.title: Zhaozhou’s “Wu”
satellites.evidence: Asked whether a dog has Buddha-nature, Zhaozhou answers 無. The Wumenguan presents the word not as a factual “no” but as a gate (關) that halts conceptual calculation.
satellites.caveat: A use of 無 inside Chinese Buddhism, not a translation of a Sanskrit term.
